la:noun:lacrima.gloss: a tear (drop of liquid from crying)
senses: a tear (drop of liquid from crying)
a tear or gumdrop exuding from plants
la:noun:lacrima.html:
lā^crĭma (archaic lacrŭma, not lacrўma, lachryma; old form dacrĭma, freq. in Livius Andronicus, acc. to Paul. ex Müll.;
v. the letter D), ae, f.
dacru-ma, kindred with Gr. δάκρυ; Sanscr. asru for dasru; Goth. tah-ja; Engl. tear; Germ. Zaehre; cf. the Sanscr. root dans and Gr. δάκ-νω, to bite
, a tear.
Lit.: meae in quem lacrumae guttatim cadunt, Enn. ap. (Trag. v. 238 Vahl.): miserae, (Trag. v. 168 id.): lacrimas effundere,: cito arescit lacrima, praesertim in alienis malis,: lacrimas dare ignoto,to shed a tear, to weep for,: lacrumas mi haec, quom video, eliciunt, quia, etc.,: ut mi excivisti lacrumas,: homini lacrumae cadunt quasi puero gaudio,tears fall from his eyes for joy, he sheds tears of joy,: lacrimis oculos suffusa nitentes,her brilliant eyes moistened with tears,: neque prae lacrimis jam loqui possum,cannot speak for tears,; cf. : lacrimas non tenere,not withhold tears, not restrain them,: tradere se lacrimis et tristitiae,: lacrimis confici,: multis cum lacrimis obsecrare,: manantibus prae gaudio lacrimis,shedding tears of joy,: lacrimis semper paratis,: lacrumae confictae dolis,: diu cohibitae lacrimae prorumpunt,tears long restrained break forth,: fatiscere in lacrimas,to dissolve in tears,: lacrumis opplet os totum sibi,: lacrimas effundere,to shed,; : profundere,: fundere,: mittere,to let flow,; but lacrimas mitte,away with tears,: lacrimae siccentur protinus,: dare,: ciere,to cause to flow,: movere,: commovere,: cohibere,: per lacrimas effundere bilem,: ciere,: lacrumas excussit mihi,forced from me,: quis talia fando temperet a lacrimis,: abstersis lacrimis,: absterget Deus omnem lacrymam ab oculis,.—Prov.: hinc illae lacrumae,; imitated by , and ; cf.: inde irae et lacrimae,.—
Transf., a tear or gum-drop which exudes from plants: narcissi,: arborum,; ; vitium, 3, § 3; .

la:verb:lacrimo.html:
lā^crĭmo (arch. lacrŭmo; not lacrў-), āvi, ātum, 1, v. n., and lacrĭmor, ātus, 1, v. dep.
lacrima
,
to shed tears, to weep (syn.: fleo, ploro; class.).
Lit.
Form lacrimo: ne lacruma, patrue,: nequeo quin lacrumem,: te lacrimasse moleste ferebam,; : lacrumo gaudio,: quid tu igitur lacrumas?: lacrumo, quae posthac futura'st vita,: ecquis fuit quin lacrimaret?: quia oculi sunt tibi lacrumantes, eo rogavi,: flentes, lacrumantes, Enn. ap. P. (Ann. v. 107 Vahl.); cf. id. ap. P. (Ann. v. 175 id.): oculis lacrimantibus,: multa super nata lacrimans,.—Impers. pass.: lacrimandum est,.—
Form lacrimor (postclass.), ; ; ; ; —
Act., to beweep, bewail, lament a thing (very rare): num id lacrumat virgo?; cf.: lacrimo quae posthac futura est vita, quom,: Argos exsequiis lacrimandus eat, (but illacrimarit is the true reading, ); cf. also the foll. no.—
Transf., to weep, drop, distil, of plants which exude a gum (poet. and post-Aug.): lacrimantes calami,: lacrimat sua gaudia palmes, Ven. Carm. 3, 9, 18: lacrimatas cortice myrrhas,dropped, distilled,.
la:verb:lacrimo.inflection: āvi, ātum, 1, v. n., ātus, 1, v. dep.

la:noun:lacuna.gloss: a hole, pit, ditch; (especially) a pool, pond
senses: a hole, pit, ditch; (especially) a pool, pond
a gap, void, defect, want, loss
la:noun:lacuna.html:
lăcūna (collateral form lŭcūna; cf. Lachm. ad Lucr. vol. 2, p. 205; lăcūnā-tūra, Hildebrand;
v.infra), ae, f.
lacus
, a ditch, pit, hole; esp. a place where water collects, a pool, pond.
Lit. (mostly poet.): lacuna, id est aquae collectio, a lacu derivatur, quam alii lamam, alii lustrum dicunt, Paul. ex Müll.: vastae,: vastae Orci,; : cavae,; .—Poet.: salsae,i. e. the sea,; ; also, Neptuniae,: caecas lustravit luce lacunas,.—
In gen., a hollow, cavity, opening, chasm, cleft: cum supercilia cana, et sub ea lacunae, dicunt, eum equum habere annos sedecim,; ; cf.: atque lacunarum fuerant vestigia cuique,; : labrum superius sub ipsa medietate narium lacuna quadam levi, quasi valle, signavit deus,: genae teretes ac medio mento lacuna,a dimple, (Hildebr., lacunatura).—
Trop., a gap, void, defect, want, loss (rare but class.): est, qui expleas duplicem istam lacunam,to fill up the double void,: ut illam lacunam rei familiaris expleant,: lacuna in auro,: illa labes et quasi lacuna famae,.

la:verb:lacuno.html:
lăcūno, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.
lacuna
. *
To hollow out, to fret or pit: lacunati tori,.—
To panel like a lacunar: summa lacunabant alterno murice conchae,.

la:verb:lacio.html:
lăcĭo, ĕre, v. a.
v. laqueus
,
to entice, allure: lacit, in fraudem inducit. Inde est allicere et lacessere; inde lactat, illectat, delectat, oblectat, Paul. ex Müll.; cf.: lacit, decipiendo inducit. Lax etenim fraus est,

la:verb:lacesso.gloss: to excite, provoke, challenge, exasperate, harass or irritate
senses: to excite, provoke, challenge, exasperate, harass or irritate
la:verb:lacesso.html:
lăcesso, īvi or ĭi, ītum, 3 (
inf. pass. lacessiri, ; ; : lacessi,; : lacessientium,: lacessiebant,), v. a.
lacio; v. Roby, 1, § 625
, to excite, provoke, challenge, exasperate, irritate (syn.: irrito, provoco).
Lit.: aliquem ferro,: sponsione me homo promtus lacessivit,: tu ultro me maledictis lacessisti,: me amabis et scripto aliquo lacesses,by writing, force me to write in return,: vetus si poeta non lacessisset prior,: hostes proelio,i. e. to attack, assail,: aliquem bello,: Aeduos injuriā,: nos te nulla lacessiimus injuria,: Saguntini nec lacessentes nec lacessiti,: aliquos lacessiturus bello,; : quorum alter relictus, alter lacessitus,: quid tam necessarium quam tenere semper arma, quibus ... to ulcisci lacessitus,: ne rudis agminum sponsus lacessat leonem,: Caesar neque cedentes tanto collis ascensu lacessendos judicabat,: aliquem capitaliter,to make a deadly attack upon one,: (corpora) quae feriunt oculorum acies visumque lacessunt,to strike, meet,; ; cf. : nares odor lacessit,: fores nondum reserati carceris acer nunc pede nunc ipsa fronte lacessit Equus,.—Poet.: aëra Sole lacessita ( = percussa radiis solis),struck with the sunbeams' glitter,; cf. vindemia pluviisque aut ventis lacessita,.—
Transf., in gen.
To urge, arouse, excite, stimulate, shake, move: a quo non modo impulsi sumus ad philosophas scriptiones, verum Etiam lacessiti,: ad scribendum,: ad pugnam,: usus luxuriantis aetatis signaturas pretiosis gemmis coepit insculpere, et certatim haec omnis imitatio lacessivit,: aurigae manibusque lacessunt Pectora plausa cavis, pat them on their breasts (in order to animate them), : pugnam,: bella,: ne quemquam voce lacessas,: his se stimulis dolor ipse lacessit,: Nilus spuma astra lacessit,: taurus lacessit campum,: clamore sidera,: deos (precibus),to assail, importune,: pelagus carinā,to stir, chafe,.—
To call forth, arouse, produce: sermones,: ferrum,.

senses: a tank, tub, sink, vat, wine-vat
la:noun:lacus.html:
lăcus, ūs (
gen. laci, ; ; ; ; dat. and abl. plur. lacis, : lacibus,; usually lacubus,), m.
root lak, to tear; Gr. λάκος, λακερός, λάκκος; Lat. lacer, lacinia, lacuna, lāma; cf. lacerna; originally any thing hollow, hence
.
A large vessel for liquids, a basin, tank, tub; esp. a vat into which the wine flowed from the press, ; ; : tu quoque devotos, Bacche, relinque lacus,: de lacubus proxima musta tuis,; a tank of water, in which heated metal was cooled: alii stridentia tingunt Aera lacu,: gelido ceu quondam lamina candens tincta lacu, stridit,: ferrum, igne rubens ... lacubus demittit,.—Hence,
Transf.: oratio quasi de musto ac lacu fervida,i. e. still new, that has not done fermenting,.—
A large body of water which rises and falls (opp. stagnum, a standing pool), a lake, pond: agri, aedificia, lacus, stagna,: exhalant lacus nebulam,: deae, quae illos Hennenses lacus lucosque incolitis,; cf. 2, 4, 48, § 107: Averni,; : Albanus,: Fucinus,: dicebar sicco vilior esse lacu, (3, 6), 12: ad spurcos lacus,.—Poet., of a river: deinde lacu fluvius se condidit alto Ima petens,; cf. v. 74; of the Styx,; 238; 393.—
A large reservoir for water, a basin, tank, cistern (of which there were a great number in Rome), ; ; ; : a furno redeuntes lacuque,.—A place called Lacus: garruli et malevoli supra Lacum, at the pond (perh. Lacus Curtius or Lacus Juturnae), .—Prov.: siccus lacus, for something useless, (3, 6, 12).—
A hole in which lime is slacked, a lime-hole, .—
One of the bins or receptacles for pulse in a granary: sed et lacubus distinguuntur granaria, ut separatim quaeque legumina ponantur,.—
A den or cave for lions: labitur in lacum leonum,; .—
The pit, the place of the dead (cf. II. fin. supra): salvasti me a descendentibus in lacum,.—
For lacunar, a panel in a ceiling (ante-class.): resultant aedesque lacusque, Lucil. ap. .

la:noun:Lacedaemon.html:
Lăcĕdaemō^n (nom.Lăcĕdaemo, ; ), ŏnis, f., = Λακεδαίμων,
the city of Lacedæmon or Sparta, near the modern Mistra: dura,; : patiens,; gen. Lacedaemonis moenia, : obsidio,; acc. Lacedaemonem, ; acc. Graec. Laceuaemona, ; abl. Lacedaemone, ; locat. Lacedaemoni, Nep. praef. 4.—
Hence,
Lăcĕdaemŏnes, um, m., the Lacedæmonians: gemini illi reges Lacedaemones Heraclidae,.—
Lăcĕdaemŏnĭus, a, um, adj., Lacedæmonian, Spartan: mulier, i. e. Helen, Enn. ap. Div. 1, 50, 114 (Trag. v. 93 Vahl.): Tarentum,i. e. founded by Spartans,; : Galesus,that flows near Tarentum,: marmor,: orbis,i. e. floor of Laconian marble,.—Subst.: Lăcĕdaemŏnĭi, ōrum, m., the Lacedæmonians, Spartans, ; ; et saep. —Sing.: Lacedaimonius quidam,; .

la:adj:lacrimabilis.html:
lăcrĭmābĭlis (lacrŭm-), e, adj.
lacrima
.
Worthy of tears, lamentable, mournful (poet. and post-class.): vixque tenet lacrimas, quia nil lacrimabile cernit,: gemitus,: bellum,; opp. felix, Am. Vict. Epit. 42, 15: nomen,.—
Tear-like: destillatio,: vox,tearful,.—Comp.: lacrimabilior series,, Serm. 17, 2: quid lacrimabilius hac stultitia, , 6.—Adv.: lăcrĭmābĭlĭter, with tears, mournfully (late Lat.), .

la:verb:lacero.html:
lăcĕro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.
lacer
,
to tear to pieces, to mangle, rend, mutilate, lacerate (class., esp. in the trop. sense; syn.: lanio, discerpo).
Lit.: quin spolies, mutiles, laceres quemquam nacta sis,: lacerat lacertum Largi mordax Memmius, Crass. ap. : corpus uti volucres lacerent in morte feraeque,: membra aliena,; cf.: lacerato corpore, Enn. ap. (Trag. v. 95 Vahl.): morsu viscera, Cic. poët. Tusc. 2, 8: ora, comas, vestem lacerat,: amictus,: genas,: verbere terga,: Tum autem Syrum impulsorem, vah, quibus illum lacerarem modis,: tergum virgis,; : unguibus cavos recessus luminum,: quid miserum laceras?: ferro,: loricam,: lacerari morsibus saevis canum, : ferae corpus lacerabant,: carnes dentibus,; .—
Esp.
To break up, to wreck, shatter: navem Ulixis,: majorem partem classis,: naves,: navigia,: lecticam,.—
To cut up, carve: obsonium,: anserem,; .—
To waste, plunder: cum Hannibal terram Italiam laceraret atque vexaret, Cato ap. : orbem,.—
Trop.
To tear to pieces with words, to censure, asperse, abuse, rail at: obtrectatio invidiaque, quae solet lacerare plerosque,: optimum virum verborum contumeliis,: aliquem probris,: Pompeium dempto metu lacerant, Dietsch: meque vosque male dictis,: famam alicujus,to slander, calumniate,: alicujus carmina,: lacerari crebro vulgi rumore,.—
To distress, torture, pain, afflict: intolerabili dolore lacerari,: quam omni crudelitate lacerastis,: quid laceras pectora nostra morā?: meus me maeror cottidianus lacerat et conficit,; cf.: aegritudo lacerat, exest animum planeque conficit,.—
To ruin, destroy, dissipate, squander, waste: male suadendo et lustris lacerant homines,: patriam omni scelere,: bonorum emptores, ut carnifices, ad reliquias vitae lacerandas et distrahendas,to scatter, disperse,: pecuniam,to squander,: lacerari valde suam rem,; cf.: bona patria manu, ventre,to lavish, squander,: diem,to waste,; .

la:adj:lacer.html:
lăcer (lăcĕrus quoted by

P.), ĕra, ĕrum, adj.

root λακ-, to tear; Gr. λακερός, torn; λάκκος, lake; Lat. lacero, lacus, lacuna, lāma; Irish, loch; Engl. lake
,
mangled, lacerated, torn to pieces.
Lit. (not in Cic. or Cæs.): homo,: corpus,; : corpus verberibus,: cui quod membrum lacerum laesumve est, Masur. Sab. ap. : Deiphobum lacerum crudeliter ora,mutilated,; so, artus avolsaque membra et funus lacerum tellus habet,.—Of the hair: nec modus aut pennis, laceris aut crinibus, ignem spargere,; ; : vestis,: tectorum vestigia lacera et semusta,: puppis,: insignia,: lacerae unguibus venae,.—
Trop. (postAug. and very rare): sparsas, atque, ut ita dicam, laceras gentilitates colligere atque conectere,families rent and scattered,.—Poet.: castra,an army that has lost its general,: lacerae domus artus componere,.—*
Transf., act., rending, lacerating (for lacerans): morsus,.

la:noun:lac.html:
lac, lactis (nom.lacte, Enn. ap. ; ; Ritschl
N. cr. al.; and lact, ; ; masc. acc. lactem, ; init.; but dub. in , where Hertz reads lacte), n.
Gr. γάλα, gen. γάλακτ-ος
, milk.
Lit.: dulci repletur lacte,: cum lacte nutricis errorem suxisse,: lacte vivere,: lac mihi non aestate novum, non frigore defit,: concretum vimine querno lac,: lactis inopia ... abundantia,: a lacte cunisque,from the cradle, from infancy,: lac pressum,cheese,: coagulatum,.—Prov.: tam similem quam lacte lacti'st,as like as one egg is to another,; cf.: neque lac lacti magis est simile,; : lac gallinaceum, chicken's milk, of something very rare, Plin. N. H. praef. § 23; : qui plus lactis quam sanguinis habet,of tender age,.—
Trop., for something sweet, pleasant: in melle sunt linguae sitae nostrae atque orationes, lacteque; corda felle sunt lita,: ut mentes ... satiari velut quodam jucundioris disciplinae lacte patiantur,.—
Transf.
Milky juice, milk of plants: herbae, nigri cum lacte veneni,: herbarum,: tenero dum lacte, quod intro est, id. Nux, 95: ficulneum,: caprifici,.—
Milk-white color (poet.): candidus taurus ... una fuit labes; cetera lactis erant,.

la:verb:lacteo.gloss: to suckle milk; to be a suckling
senses: to suckle milk; to be a suckling
to contain milk or sap, to be milky or sappy
la:verb:lacteo.html:
lactĕo, ēre (used almost exclusively in the
part. pres.), v. a.
lac
.
To suck milk, to be a suckling: Romulus parvus atque lactens, uberibus lupinis inhians,; so, lactens Juppiter puer,: vitulus,; : lactens hostia,; also absol.: lactentibus rem divinam facere,.— Poet.: viscera lactentia,i. e. sucking children, sucklings,.—Of the spring: tener et lactens (sc. annus),. —
To contain milk or sap, to be milky, sappy, juicy: verno tempore, cum lactent novella virentia,; cf.: nam sata, vere novo, teneris lactentia sucis,: frumenta in viridi stipula lactentia turgent,: lactuca lactens,.—Subst.: lactentĭa, ium, n., milk-food, milk-dishes, .

la:noun:lacertus.gloss: The muscular part of the upper arm, including the shoulder, biceps, and triceps.
senses: The muscular part of the upper arm, including the shoulder, biceps, and triceps.
la:noun:lacertus.html:
lăcertus, i, m.,
the muscular part of the arm, from the shoulder to the elbow, the upper arm.
Lit., opp. bracchium, the forearm, ; cf.: laudat digitosque manusque, Bracchiaque et nudos mediā plus parte lacertos,; and: subjecta lacertis brachia sunt,; cf. also : brachia quoque et lacertos auro colunt,.—
Transf.
The arm (esp. as brawny, muscular): nam scutum gladium galeam in onere nostri milites non plus numerant quam umeros, lacertos, manus,: Milo Crotoniates nobilitatus ex lateribus et lacertis suis,: excusso lacerto telum torquere,; (3, 15), 37: lacertos collo imponere,: lacerto jaculari,: amplecti,: candida cingantur colla lacertis,: laevus,; : adducto contortum hastile lacerto immittit,: secto requiem sperare lacerto,. —Of bees: spicula exacuunt rostris, aptantque lacertos,i. e. make trial of,.—
Transf.
A blow or cast from a strong arm, ; .—
Trop., muscular power, muscle, strength, military force: in Lysia saepe sunt lacerti, sic ut fieri nihil possit valentius,: hastas oratoris lacertis viribusque torquere,: me civilis tulit aestus in arma, Caesaris Augusti non responsura lacertis,; Flor. prooem. § 8: viribus confisus admirandisque lacertis,.

lăcerna, ae, f.
cf. Gr. ῥάκος, and lacer
,
a kind of cloak which the Romans wore over the toga on journeys, or in damp and cold weather. To wear a lacerna in common was regarded as disgraceful: cum calceis et toga, nullis nec Gallicis nec lacerna,: negotium aedilibus dedit, ne quem paterenter in foro circove, nisi positis lacernis, togatum consistere,: cum Gallicis, inquit, et lacerna cucurristi,. Worn in the theatre as a protection against the weather, but thrown off on the appearance of the emperor, ; lemm. Sometimes wrapped around the head: odoratum caput obscurante lacerna,; . Usually of white cloth, rarely black, sqq.; ; v. also : foeda et scissa,. Also used in the army, ; ; ; : comitem trita donare lacerna,; cf. Becker's Gallus, 3, p. 123 sq.; and v. Dict. Antiq. s. v.
